name: GRAIL (Ebb and Flow)
short_status: Complete: twin orbiters mapped the Moon's gravity through 2012, then struck a far-northern mountain on Dec 17, 2012; NASA named the site for Sally Ride.
tagline: NASA · United States · Orbiter · 2011 · The robotic return Success
stats: total mission cost including launch and operations
average crustal thickness GRAIL measured, 10 to 20 km thinner than earlier estimates
MoonKAM images taken on targets picked by middle school students
speed at which Ebb and Flow struck the mountain named for Sally Ride

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 10 September 2011, 13:08:52 UT, on a Delta II 7920H (Heavy) from Space Launch Complex 17B, Cape Canaveral

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: Identical twins on Lockheed Martin's XSS-11-derived bus: 307 kg fueled, 201 kg dry, with a science payload derived from the GRACE Earth-gravity mission

facts.label: Leadership
facts.value: Principal investigator Maria Zuber (MIT), the first woman to lead a robotic planetary mission for NASA; project management at JPL

facts.label: Cruise and arrival
facts.value: 3.5-month low-energy cruise via the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 1; Ebb entered lunar orbit 31 December 2011, Flow on 1 January 2012

facts.label: Names
facts.value: Ebb and Flow, announced 17 January 2012, proposed by Nina DiMauro's fourth-grade class at Emily Dickinson Elementary in Bozeman, Montana, winners of a contest that drew nearly 900 classrooms and over 11,000 students

facts.label: Technique
facts.value: Lunar Gravity Ranging System: a Ka-band radio link between the twins measured changes in their separation velocity to about 4.5 micrometers per second

facts.label: Mapping campaigns
facts.value: Primary mapping March to 29 May 2012 from about 55 km altitude in three 27.3-day cycles; extended mission August 30 to 14 December 2012 at 23 km average, dipping to 11 km

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: About $496.2 million total, covering spacecraft development, instruments, launch services, operations and science processing

facts.label: Headline result
facts.value: The highest-resolution gravity map of any celestial body at the time, released 5 December 2012, resolving mascons and gravity signatures of craters, rilles and mountains

facts.label: Crust results
facts.value: Average crustal thickness of 34 to 43 km, 10 to 20 km thinner than previously thought, plus buried linear dikes hundreds of kilometers long (Science, December 2012)

facts.label: MoonKAM
facts.value: Each twin carried a MoonKAM education camera; imaging targets were proposed by middle school students, who received more than 115,000 images through the program run by Sally Ride Science

facts.label: Impact and naming
facts.value: 17 December 2012, at 22:28:51 and 22:29:21 UTC, both twins hit the southern face of a 2.5 km-tall mountain near Goldschmidt crater at 1.7 km/s; NASA named the location the Sally K. Ride Impact Site the same day

timeline: Launch at 13:08:52 UT on a Delta II Heavy from Cape Canaveral SLC-17B, the last Delta II to fly from the Cape
Ebb (GRAIL-A) enters lunar orbit on New Year's Eve after the 3.5-month low-energy cruise
Flow (GRAIL-B) joins its twin in lunar orbit on New Year's Day
GRAIL-A and GRAIL-B become Ebb and Flow, names proposed by Bozeman, Montana fourth graders
Mar 2012
Primary gravity mapping begins from about 55 km; the first student-commanded MoonKAM images come down mid-month
Primary mission complete after three full mapping cycles
Extended mission mapping begins at 23 km average altitude, half the primary height, later dipping to 11 km
NASA releases the gravity map and three Science papers: a thinner, battered crust and giant buried dikes
Extended mission science collection ends; the nearly empty twins are set up for disposal
Final depletion burns (Ebb 4 min 3 s, Flow 5 min 7 s), then both twins strike the mountainside at 1.7 km/s, 22:28:51 and 22:29:21 UTC; NASA names the site for Sally Ride
LROC stereo images taken this day locate both impact craters, about 5 m across and 2,210 m apart, each with odd dark ejecta
LRO's LAMP spectrograph reports mercury and atomic hydrogen in the impact plumes it watched rise into sunlight
GRAIL data solve the 45-year mascon mystery: dense gravity bumps are the signature of ancient giant impacts into a hotter Moon
